the ‘disabled’ strain of E. coli, χ1776, was as pathogenic as its parent K12 strain when injected into mice by various routes.
the pathogenicity of conventional E. coli K-12 DO-11 is similar to that of the ‘disabled’, non-colonizing E. coli χ 1776, when introduced parenterally.

the development of ‘disabled’, recombinant DNA E. coli for use in the laboratory.
the study of the pathogenicity of E. coli strains which are not able to persist in the intestines of mice, and which are therefore of little danger to man or animal in their normal habitat.
the development of a system for testing the safety of recombinant DNA constructs in animals.

E. coli K-12 strains, even if disabled, retain a significant degree of pathogenicity.
, although the ‘disabled’ strains have been shown to be less pathogenic, they are nevertheless capable of producing disease.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ‘disabled’ strain of E. coli χ 1776, although it is incapable of colonising the intestinal tract of normal mice, can nevertheless cause death by parenteral inoculation.
the ‘disabled’ strain χ1776 is not significantly different from its parental strain K12 DO- 11 in terms of pathogenicity when introduced parenterally into mice.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the pathogenicity of E. coli is not necessarily reduced by the loss of the ability to survive and colonize outside the host, and that it is therefore important to investigate the pathogenicity in vivo of all E. coli strains used in recombinant DNA experiments.
the use of ‘disabled’ E. coli K12 strains as vehicles for recombinant-DNA experiments does not necessarily imply a reduced risk of accidental infection.
the ‘disabled’ strains are as pathogenic as their parent strains, and that they should be treated with the same care and precautions in the laboratory as any pathogenic organism.
